title: To Grow, a Leader Needs to Be Inauthentic
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article makes a counterintuitive claim: leadership authenticity is defined by consistent behavior over time, not internal feelings, which means any leader attempting to build a genuinely new habit is, by definition, acting inauthentically at first. It explains that team members read authenticity through repeated action, so a leader trying a new behavior is initially met with suspicion rather than credit, since colleagues assume the change is a deliberate influence tactic rather than a real shift. The piece argues this resistance period is unavoidable and that leaders who persist only because they believe the new behavior reflects their real values are the ones who sustain the change. It frames this temporary inauthenticity as a necessary, uncomfortable phase of genuine leadership growth rather than a contradiction to avoid.
points: Authenticity is defined by what leaders consistently do, not by what they feel or intend, meaning new behavior always starts out looking "inauthentic."
Team members initially treat any new leadership behavior with suspicion, assuming it's a deliberate influence tactic rather than genuine change.
The leaders most likely to sustain a new behavior are those doing it because it reflects their real values, not to chase quick results.
Growth in leadership style depends on tolerating a period of perceived inauthenticity and resistance that can't be skipped.
quotes: Contrary to popular leadership wisdom, authenticity is not a reflection of how leaders display what is in their hearts or heads.
We know leaders for what they do, not for how they think or feel.
The reality is that any time a leader attempts to incorporate a new behavior they have not previously performed consistently, they are acting inauthentically in the eyes of those they lead.
The team’s initial conclusion is that the leader must be doing something new to have an “effect” or to influence others, which is not to be rewarded with acceptance or appreciation.
But without this period of inauthenticity and resistance, leaders can’t grow and develop.
